passage: Counsellor's log, 14 August. Jeevan (Class 10) came in at lunch, uneasy. He said a rumour has gone round that Mrs Rashmi Nair, the maths teacher, marks down anyone who takes outside tuition. He first heard it as a joke two weeks ago. Now, he said, 'Nobody even asks if it's true. People have changed tuitions because of it.' He has watched classmates repeat the same story with new 'proof' each time: a low mark here, a stern look there. He admitted he almost believes it himself, because he has heard it so often. We talked about where it started; he couldn't name anyone who knew. Next step: I will speak with the principal and with Mrs Nair today, and plan a class talk on how rumours grow.

qa.q: What was the rumour about Mrs Rashmi Nair?
qa.a: That she marks down anyone who takes outside tuition.

qa.q: What was Jeevan worried about on coming to the counsellor?
qa.a: Jeevan was uneasy that nobody questioned the rumour any more, and that even Jeevan was starting to believe it just from hearing it so often.

qa.q: What did the counsellor choose to do after listening, and why was it sensible?
qa.a: The counsellor planned to speak with the principal and Mrs Nair that day and hold a class talk, so the teacher could respond and students could see how repetition builds belief.

qa.q: What might this rumour be like for Mrs Nair?
qa.a: Mrs Nair may notice students treating her with suspicion and switching tuitions without knowing why, which could feel unfair and hurtful.

grounding: A counsellor's note records a student noticing a rumour about a teacher harden into accepted fact through repetition.

passage:
12 Nov
Weird day. Two weeks ago Sunaina said, just guessing, that Mr Pinto, the new geography teacher, 'probably' got thrown out of his last school. Today I heard it five times. On the bus it was 'he was fired.' In the canteen it was 'he was fired for shouting at a kid.' By last period, Rehan swore his cousin 'knows someone' from that school. Nobody said 'probably' any more. When Mr Pinto raised his voice over the fans, the whole row went silent and swapped looks, like he'd proved something.
I asked Sunaina if she remembered starting it. She went red. 'I didn't mean it like that.'
Now I don't know how to un-start it.
— Nandini

qa.q: How many times did Nandini hear the rumour today?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling on going red?
qa.a: Sunaina seemed embarrassed and perhaps guilty, realising a casual guess had turned into something everyone believed.

qa.q: Now that the source is clear, what could Nandini choose to do?
qa.a: Nandini could tell classmates the story began as a guess and ask a trusted teacher or counsellor for help, since Mr Pinto is being judged unfairly.

qa.q: How might Mr Pinto experience the row going silent?
qa.a: Mr Pinto may sense the class is suddenly wary without knowing why, which could make a new job feel lonely and confusing.

grounding: A student's diary tracks a guess about a teacher turning into accepted fact as each retelling adds certainty.

passage: The shared jeep from Wadgaon to the high school in the kasba took forty minutes, long enough for a story to grow. On Monday, Francis said he'd heard that Kulkarni Madam kept the library fund for herself. He said "heard" twice. On Tuesday, two girls from Class 9 said she had bought a new scooter with it. On Wednesday nobody said "heard" any more. Samir, fifteen, watched from his corner seat as the story went back and forth like a bag of peanuts. By Friday, students stopped returning library books to her desk and left them with the peon instead. Samir had seen her scooter. It was old and dented. He opened his mouth to say so, then looked at the full jeep and shut it.

qa.q: How long did the shared jeep ride take?
qa.a: It took forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Samir shut his mouth after opening it to speak?
qa.a: He seemed to feel the whole jeep already treated the story as fact, and was afraid of looking foolish for questioning it.

qa.q: What small step could Samir take after that ride?
qa.a: He could quietly tell Francis what he knew about the old, dented scooter, or ask where the story first came from, starting with one person.

qa.q: What might it be like for Kulkarni Madam when students start leaving books with the peon?
qa.a: She might feel hurt and confused, noticing students avoid her without knowing why, with no way to answer a rumour no one says to her face.

grounding: A student watches a rumour about a teacher harden into accepted fact through repetition.

passage: At the upper school in Aarhus, the story about Mr Holm started as a joke. Valentina, new that term from Madrid, said in chemistry that he handled the burner "like someone who's blown up a lab before." Everyone laughed. The next week, Ulla heard in the cloakroom that he actually had blown up a lab at his old school and been sacked. Then that a student had been hurt. Then a name for the student. Ulla, sixteen, noticed that each version came with more detail and less doubt. Nobody asked Mr Holm. People flinched now when he lit the burner. When Ulla mentioned Valentina's joke, a girl from her class said, "No, it's true, everyone knows." Valentina, sitting nearby, looked uneasy and stayed quiet.

qa.q: What did Valentina first say about Mr Holm?
qa.a: Valentina said he handled the burner "like someone who's blown up a lab before."

qa.q: What might Valentina's uneasy silence reveal about how she felt?
qa.a: Valentina seemed to realise the joke had turned into a "fact" about a real teacher, and may have felt guilty but unsure how to take it back.

qa.q: What could Ulla do, since she knows where the story started?
qa.a: Ulla could calmly tell a trusted teacher, or the class, that it began as a joke, and ask whether anyone actually knows more.

qa.q: How might Mr Holm experience a class that flinches when he lights the burner?
qa.a: He might feel puzzled and uneasy, sensing a distrust he can't explain because nobody has told him the rumour.

grounding: A student observes a joke about a teacher grow into an unquestioned fact with every retelling.
